title: Command
summary: Represent a request as an object so you can queue, log, or undo it.

parts.rule: A command is a value that represents an action and the data needed to perform it. An invoker can execute that value now, store it in history, queue it, or compose it with other commands. Undo is optional; when promised, the command must capture enough state to reverse its own completed change.
parts.why: A direct method call disappears as soon as it returns. Turning the request into a value makes deferred work, audit logs, keyboard bindings, macros, and undo histories possible. The cost is a class or record per meaningful action plus careful state capture, so commands are useful when operations need a lifecycle beyond one call.
parts.example: A text editor starts with buffer "cat" and the cursor at index 3. InsertText(text="s", position=3) executes by inserting one character, producing "cats". The editor pushes that command onto its undo stack. undo() removes exactly one character at index 3, returning to "cat"; redo() executes the same command again. DeleteRange(start=1, length=2) needs more information: before deleting "at", it stores the removed text inside the command so undo() can restore it. A MacroCommand containing InsertText("!", 4) and ApplyBold(0, 4) executes children in order and undoes them in reverse order. The receiver—the document—still owns the actual mutation rules; the command stores intent and reversal data. For queued billing work, ChargeCard(commandId=847, invoiceId=21, cents=5000) can be serialized and retried. The handler records commandId 847 before charging so a redelivery does not charge twice. That is still a command, but its reversal may be a separate Refund command rather than pretending a remote charge can be silently undone.
parts.use: Use commands when users need undo or redo, when the same action is triggered from several UI controls, or when an operation must be logged, scheduled, or retried as data. Keep each command focused on one domain action and make its inputs explicit enough to replay safely.
parts.refuse: Use a direct function call when nothing needs to store or manage the action. Do not claim undo if the command failed halfway or discarded the previous state. Avoid commands that grab arbitrary global objects during execution; they are hard to replay and test. Observer publishes completed events, while command represents an instruction—do not swap those meanings.

body:
Rule. A command is a value that represents an action and the data needed to perform it. An invoker can execute that value now, store it in history, queue it, or compose it with other commands. Undo is optional; when promised, the command must capture enough state to reverse its own completed change.

Why it matters. A direct method call disappears as soon as it returns. Turning the request into a value makes deferred work, audit logs, keyboard bindings, macros, and undo histories possible. The cost is a class or record per meaningful action plus careful state capture, so commands are useful when operations need a lifecycle beyond one call.

Worked example. A text editor starts with buffer "cat" and the cursor at index 3. InsertText(text="s", position=3) executes by inserting one character, producing "cats". The editor pushes that command onto its undo stack. undo() removes exactly one character at index 3, returning to "cat"; redo() executes the same command again. DeleteRange(start=1, length=2) needs more information: before deleting "at", it stores the removed text inside the command so undo() can restore it. A MacroCommand containing InsertText("!", 4) and ApplyBold(0, 4) executes children in order and undoes them in reverse order. The receiver—the document—still owns the actual mutation rules; the command stores intent and reversal data. For queued billing work, ChargeCard(commandId=847, invoiceId=21, cents=5000) can be serialized and retried. The handler records commandId 847 before charging so a redelivery does not charge twice. That is still a command, but its reversal may be a separate Refund command rather than pretending a remote charge can be silently undone.

[[diagram:command]]

When to use. Use commands when users need undo or redo, when the same action is triggered from several UI controls, or when an operation must be logged, scheduled, or retried as data. Keep each command focused on one domain action and make its inputs explicit enough to replay safely.

When to refuse. Use a direct function call when nothing needs to store or manage the action. Do not claim undo if the command failed halfway or discarded the previous state. Avoid commands that grab arbitrary global objects during execution; they are hard to replay and test. Observer publishes completed events, while command represents an instruction—do not swap those meanings.
